reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / WHO Classification of Endocrine Tumours
clinicalPearls: A common cause of hyperthyroidism in older adults, arising in a long-standing multinodular goitre when one or more nodules become autonomously hyperfunctioning
Thyrotoxicosis is often insidious and may be 'apathetic', dominated by atrial fibrillation, weight loss, or heart failure rather than classic adrenergic features
Biochemistry shows suppressed TSH with elevated thyroid hormones, and TSH-receptor antibodies are absent because the disorder is autonomous, not autoimmune
Isotope uptake scanning demonstrates patchy uptake with multiple hot areas and suppressed internodular tissue, distinguishing it from the diffuse uptake of Graves disease
Autonomy commonly reflects accumulated activating TSH-receptor mutations within nodules developing over years of goitrous change
A large retrosternal goitre can produce compressive symptoms and positional airway narrowing, which surgery addresses better than radioactive iodine
Iodine loads from contrast media or amiodarone frequently precipitate overt thyrotoxicosis in these autonomous glands
reference.pathophysiology: Toxic multinodular goitre develops when a long-standing multinodular goitre acquires foci of autonomous function. Over time, subpopulations of follicular cells accumulate somatic activating mutations, particularly of the TSH receptor, so that individual nodules secrete thyroid hormone independently of TSH. As autonomous mass increases, circulating thyroid hormone rises and suppresses pituitary TSH, silencing the internodular parenchyma and producing the characteristic patchy scintigraphic pattern. Because the autonomous tissue avidly traps iodine, exposure to iodinated contrast or iodine-rich drugs such as amiodarone can abruptly increase hormone synthesis and precipitate thyrotoxicosis.
additionalInvestigations: Serum TSH with free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine to confirm thyrotoxicosis
Radioiodine or technetium uptake scan showing patchy multifocal uptake
Neck ultrasound to characterise the nodular gland and identify any dominant or suspicious nodule
Cross-sectional imaging when retrosternal extension or compression is suspected
TSH-receptor antibodies to exclude coexisting Graves disease where uncertain
Review of iodine exposure including contrast and amiodarone
redFlags: New atrial fibrillation, heart failure, or thromboembolism from occult thyrotoxicosis in an older patient
Thyroid storm features such as fever, delirium, and cardiovascular collapse
Compressive airway symptoms or stridor from a large or retrosternal goitre
Severe thyrotoxicosis precipitated by iodinated contrast or amiodarone
reference.prognosis: With definitive treatment by radioactive iodine or surgery the outlook is good; untreated disease, especially in the elderly, carries substantial cardiovascular and bone morbidity, and large goitres may cause progressive compression.
pitfalls: Overlooking apathetic thyrotoxicosis presenting only as atrial fibrillation or weight loss in an older patient
Administering iodinated contrast or amiodarone without recognising the risk of precipitating thyrotoxicosis
Choosing radioactive iodine for a large compressive or retrosternal goitre better managed surgically
Assuming diffuse Graves-type uptake and missing the patchy autonomous pattern on scanning
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
